articles.title_orig: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
articles.title_zh: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
articles.content_orig:
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.
Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.
Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) , which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.
So why is Beijing not eager?
New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.
Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.
New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.
The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.
The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.
Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.
Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.
“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that same month said Trump made it clear that “to have true arms control in the 21st century, it’s impossible to do something that doesn’t include China because of their vast and rapidly growing stockpile”.
Washington also wants a successor treaty to address weapons not covered by New START.
DiNanno has said a new agreement would have to “account [for] all Russian nuclear weapons, both novel and existing strategic systems and [address] the breakout growth of Chinese nuclear weapons stockpiles”.
Beijing’s unwillingness is largely due to the sheer disparity of warheads it currently possesses when compared with the US and Russia.
It has an estimated 620 of them, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), well below the 800 cap each for Russia and the US under New START. Moscow and Washington now have more than 5,000 each, according to SIPRI data. While the US has retired a third of its nuclear warheads so far, Russia has retired less than a fourth.
China’s nuclear arsenal, however, is growing faster than any country’s – by about 100 new warheads a year since 2023, according to SIPRI.
In February, when New Start expired, Chinese officials explained their opposition to joining a nuclear weapons capping agreement.
“China’s nuclear forces are not on the same level as those of the United States and Russia, and China will not participate in disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a statement at the time.
This “structural asymmetry” explains China’s reluctance to join a nuclear arms control treaty with the US and Russia alongside its own domestic restraints, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at the Institute of International Studies at China’s Fudan University.
“China maintains a declared no-first-use policy and a ‘minimum deterrence’ posture – nuclear weapons as political instruments for assured retaliation, not warfighting,” Zhao told Al Jazeera.
“From Beijing’s perspective, its arsenal is already restrained by doctrine. The potential US-Russia-China treaty would cap its insurance while imposing intrusive verification on a comparatively small force.”
He also pointed to a “credibility problem”, given the US withdrawal from a number of related treaties, such as the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which similarly seek to control missile numbers.
In China’s view, Washington has used arms control as a geopolitical instrument, Zhao said.
“Beijing’s strategic logic is that nuclear inferiority invites coercion – conventional or nuclear – while survivable second-strike capability neutralises it,” he said.
China’s smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, but so does its ability to match US capabilities, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“Chinese assessments also consider US missile defences, precision-strike capabilities and emerging technologies that could weaken its retaliatory capability,” Sun told Al Jazeera.
“An agreement limiting China’s forces while leaving those concerns untouched would have limited appeal.”
According to William Yang, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Northeast Asia, there’s no clear advantage for Beijing and any treaty would be viewed “as a mechanism designed to limit its nuclear modernisation”.
“As a result, Beijing prefers to maintain strategic autonomy in expanding its nuclear arsenal and modernising relevant defence capabilities,” Yang told Al Jazeera.
At the same time, China’s rapid nuclear expansion raises “legitimate questions about where Beijing intends to stop”, said Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong,
“It is difficult to assess China’s ultimate ambitions when it provides little transparency about its nuclear programme. We should not assume that China seeks parity, but neither should we assume that its declared commitment to minimum deterrence fully explains its current build-up,” Reyes told Al Jazeera.
According to the analysts, China would engage in a trilateral framework only when the US and Russia first reduce their arsenals towards “genuine” parity.
Zhao argued that such a path could be incremental.
It could appear as a “sustained US-China strategic stability dialogue with concrete reciprocity – test moratoria, data exchanges [and] notification of major exercises”, he explained.
The negotiations would also need to address missile defence, advanced conventional weapons and emerging technologies, Sun said.
“Differentiated obligations and phased verification would offer a more workable basis than identical reductions,” he added.

articles.title_orig: China’s new home prices fall again in October; slowest annual decline in almost a year
articles.title_zh: China’s new home prices fall again in October; slowest annual decline in almost a year
articles.content_orig:
By Liangping Gao, Yukun Zhang and Ryan Woo
BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) – China’s new home prices declined again in October, albeit at the slowest annual rate in almost a year, extending a years-long slump that has eroded market confidence, sapped consumer spending ​and squeezed local government income.
Prices fell 0.1% versus September, when they also fell ‌0.1% on month, showed Reuters calculations based on data from the National Bureau of Statistics released on Monday.
They fell 2.4% versus October last year, the slowest pace of decline since November 2025. In September, prices fell 2.8% on year.
The data showed little indication of price recovery across the nation while conditions in big and small ‌cities ​continue to diverge, said analyst Zhang Dawei at Centaline Property. The ⁠number of cities with rising ⁠prices keeps shrinking, and signs of stabilisation are limited to a handful of areas, he said.
The sector, once an economic growth driver, has been the target of a slew of support measures yet has shown few signs of improvement. Analysts have said persistent price ​declines indicate the sector will likely remain a drag on the economy and that more drastic stimulus is needed.
A decline in property value shrinks homeowners’ wealth, nudging them to save instead ⁠of spend, especially amid a weak job market and ⁠slow wage growth.
Property investment, sales and new construction all continued to fall ​by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, official data showed.
For the sector ​to turn around, price stabilisation is necessary across cities, and property inventories need ‌to normalise, Lynn Song, ING chief economist for Greater China, wrote in a client note.
Smaller cities have experienced a prolonged downturn for both new and resale homes. Among the biggest cities, Shanghai alone registered both on-month and on-year price rises for both new and resale homes in October.
Resale ⁠home prices in so-called tier-one cities rose for an eighth month, indicating stability, though the trend is partly propelled by buyers opting for ready housing rather than risk waiting for projects that may ⁠not come to fruition, Zhang ‌said.
Completed homes that buyers can see and touch have become a kind ⁠of hard currency, and the “certainty premium” on resale homes is also ​showing, he ‌said.
To prop up consumer sentiment dampened by stalled housing projects, the ​government this ⁠year introduced measures to deter developers from selling homes before project completion.
Policymakers this year also introduced interest subsidies on new commercial mortgages for eligible first-time homebuyers.
Overall property investment and sales volume will likely keep falling for some time, and the sector will remain an economic drag next year, said equity analyst Jeff Zhang at Morningstar.
(Reporting by Liangping Gao, Yukun Zhang and Ryan Woo; Editing by Clarence ​Fernandez and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, the tech executive whose reported relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of international spying claims, left the company last year.
The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.
“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” the statement said.
Megaspeed also pushed back on media reports it said contained claims about its operations that “are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said.
Megaspeed, a major buyer of graphics processing units (GPUs) made by the California-based Nvidia, used to train and run frontier AI models, is facing scrutiny over its compliance with United States export controls intended to keep high-end chips out of China.
While data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand can import high-end Nvidia chips legally, US authorities have long suspected the region is a hotbed of illicit smuggling on behalf of Chinese AI developers.
Megaspeed CEO and chairman Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday that the company had retained a top US law firm to lead a “comprehensive census” of its GPUs and verify its export control compliance practices.
Unnamed US officials have accused Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO , president and board member on Thursday amid a board investigation.
Beijing has denied the allegations, describing them as “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims.
Singaporean authorities are investigating Megaspeed on suspicion of making false declarations in relation to its purchases of servers. They said last week they had previously confiscated Alice Huang’s passport for eight months as part of their inquiries.
Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that it barred Huang from re-entering the country after determining that she had provided inaccurate information to investigators to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | The New Congress Must Rein in Trump’s Dangerous China Policy
articles.title_zh: Opinion | The New Congress Must Rein in Trump’s Dangerous China Policy
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in Washington, DC, on Sept. 4, 2025.
Democrats and Republicans in the new Congress will disagree about plenty in health policy. However, they should agree that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) should be a scientific agency whose judgments hold steady no matter who occupies the White House. In January, Congress will have the chance to write that principle into law.
For decades, the scientific independence of America’s public health agencies rested on a bipartisan understanding. Presidential administrations disagreed about health policy, sometimes profoundly, but their health secretaries generally respected the expertise and established processes of agencies like the CDC and the Food and Drug Administration.
Earlier administrations of both parties—including those of Republican Secretary of Health and Human Services Alex Azar and Democratic Secretary Xavier Becerra —faced charges of political interference, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, and some had merit. But I would argue that none have even approached the scale and scope of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s interventions. The safeguards that existed were administrative policies, and a new secretary can discard them.
In June 2025, Kennedy dismissed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced them with his own appointees. No prior secretary had done this. Congress had given U.S. Health and Human Services secretaries broad authority and relied on their restraint. Restraint is a tradition, and the past year shows it can end.
To address this, Congress should pursue four priorities.
Elected leaders have a legitimate role in setting national health priorities and holding agencies accountable. That role ends where scientific judgment begins, and Congress should draw the line in statute:
Codify the advisory committee on immunization with clear membership qualifications, a transparent appointment process, and removal only for cause.
Require documented, public evidence reviews behind any major change to a scientific recommendation.
Require a secretary who departs from a formal recommendation to explain why in public, separating the scientific evidence from considerations like cost and implementation.
Protect career scientists’ ability to publish findings and communicate evidence, and create an independent office to investigate political interference, with whistleblower protections.
These rules must bind every future secretary, including those appointed by the party that controls Congress today. A protection that works against only one party’s appointees will not last.
The CDC has lost more than a quarter of its workforce since 2024. The losses include epidemiologists who investigate outbreaks, laboratory scientists who identify emerging pathogens, specialists who evaluate evidence, and professionals who work with state and local health departments. That expertise takes years to develop.
Congress should require an independent assessment of the CDC’s current capabilities and direct the agency to produce a public rebuilding plan with measurable targets for restoring essential functions. Personnel protections should support a professional scientific workforce that can serve administrations of either party. Targets should follow the agency’s mission, whatever headcount that implies.
COVID exposed confusion about the separate roles of the federal and state governments. The CDC could issue guidance, but implementation depended on state and local officials working under different laws, budgets, and political pressures.
Congress should specify what Americans can count on their national public health agency to do: investigate outbreaks when states request help, publish evidence-based guidance, and operate a national data system that state and local health departments can contribute to and draw from in near real time. It should fund those partners to participate, because the CDC’s guidance reaches Americans through their local health departments.
Scientific independence invites scrutiny, and protecting the CDC from political interference makes meaningful accountability more important. Congress should establish public measures of performance.
How effectively does the CDC identify and investigate emerging threats? How quickly does it get reliable information to states? How transparently does it evaluate evidence? How well does it communicate uncertainty and update recommendations as evidence changes?
An independent body should evaluate these questions, accounting for outcomes that depend on state and local partners. The purpose is to find weaknesses and improve performance.
With a Republican president in the White House, sweeping legislation will require bipartisan support. Congress can begin with oversight hearings, appropriations language, and independent investigations while it builds a coalition for lasting statutory protections. And they can start by pursuing common-sense, common-ground policies.
For eight decades , the CDC has protected Americans from infectious diseases and other health threats. Americans deserve a CDC whose science they can trust, whose expertise is protected, and whose ability to safeguard their health does not depend on who occupies the White House.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted efforts by other Trump administration officials to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China, sources tell Axios. Photo: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images
President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.
Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal.
Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen.
This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?"
Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic.
The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations.
Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.
Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for.
The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

articles.title_orig: Political setbacks at home complicate Trump’s China strategy
articles.title_zh: Political setbacks at home complicate Trump’s China strategy
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING/WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, reeling from a midterm election drubbing and Chinese spy allegations that have raised the stakes for his latest face-to-face with Beijing’s powerful leader, Xi Jinping.
Trump will first visit Manila for meetings with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders on Tuesday before jetting to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where he will meet the Chinese president and hold three-way discussions with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
With a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China extended to early next year, and more Trump-Xi talks due in December at the G20 in Miami, some analysts had initially billed the Shenzhen meeting as a low-stakes summit.
But a backlash against Trump’s Republican Party in this month’s midterms and criticism that his administration failed to act on intelligence that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, have muddied those expectations.
“With less reason to worry about market reactions or electoral fallout, (Trump) may be more willing to consider disruptive measures,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at the Tony Blair Institute, a London-based think tank.
Washington has already signalled such willingness ahead of the meeting, urging China to live up to its commitments made under the truce agreed between Trump and Xi a year ago.
Chinese analysts say they are particularly concerned that the Nvidia saga, including allegations that restricted semiconductors were diverted to Chinese customers, will now harden US attitudes towards China.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week there was growing consensus in Congress on further limiting Chinese access to advanced chips after the scandal, and Democrats are expected to press hard on the issue when they take over the House and Senate majorities in January.
China has said the United States has fabricated the spy narrative to justify a technological blockade.
Zhu Feng, director of the Institute of International Studies at Nanjing University, said the spat could also speed up “the decoupling of AI” between the world’s two superpowers even as they try to cooperate on mitigating the technology’s risks.
Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration said on condition of anonymity, adding that the Nvidia situation “should not really have any bearing on the trip.”
Rather than picking fresh fights with China, Trump may want to focus on legacy-building endeavours such as denuclearisation agreements with Beijing and Moscow, or securing another meeting with North Korea’s secretive leader, Kim Jong Un.
Trump sees the unprecedented summit with Xi and Putin as possibly providing movement towards an agreement on nuclear arms control. But that is a non-starter for China, which has far fewer warheads than the others, Chinese analysts said.
Trump may also seek to enlist Putin and Xi’s support in setting up a future meeting with Kim, who has close ties to the Chinese and Russian leaders.
The president will be focused on “building his legacy,” said Victor Cha at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank. A big part of that is his North Korea diplomacy, which he has devoted a lot of time to over his two terms, Cha added.
The proposed three-way meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
Such a framing is particularly worrisome for Ukraine, engaged in a four-year war with Russia. Trump is not expected to raise Ukraine at the meeting, the senior US official said.
Xi could also seek to take advantage of Trump’s political weakness after his election humbling, analysts say.
Top of Beijing’s wish list is ensuring that the US president doesn’t approve a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Trump has said he is holding the arms back as a “negotiating chip” with China.
But with China’s export engine humming, simply buying time may be enough for Beijing, said Jonathan Czin, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution, a US-based think tank.
“Xi just needs Trump to remain reluctant to revert toward a more competitive posture toward China for as long as possible. China will take whatever time it can get to fortify itself for the next round in the contest,” said Czin, who formerly worked at the Central Intelligence Agency and as director for China at the US National Security Council.
Beijing will be acutely aware that whoever succeeds Trump when his term ends in two years time, may be less accommodating, said Czin and Osman.
Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, repeatedly angered China with comments over human rights issues and a pledge that the US would defend Taiwan if Beijing attacked. Many of Trump’s potential Republican successors, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are also seen as more hawkish on China.
Both leaders will also be wary of reigniting a trade row that threatened to tank the global economy and financial markets last year, said Kurt Tong, a former senior State Department official now with the Asia Group think tank.
Despite the frustration the US has voiced on Chinese implementation of the terms of the truce, Tong expects it will be further extended beyond its January 10 expiration.
“The two sides are quite incentivized to maintain this fragile stability … despite also having some disagreements,” added senior China analyst Chim Lee at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
“They both have quite a lot to lose.”

articles.title_orig: Stock futures slip as traders brace for Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO this week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures slip as traders brace for Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO this week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures slipped Monday morning following a volatile week on Wall Street, as traders await a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic.
Nasdaq-100 futures declined 0.77%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.37%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 103 points lower, or 0.20%.
In Asia, markets were mostly lower with Japan's Nikkei 225 dropping 2.04% after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. South Korea Kospi slumped 3.48%, leading losses in the region. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.41% as well. Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.83% after downbeat key economic data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.94%.
Nvidia is set to report results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the chipmaker to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Another key catalyst is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.
European stock markets are expected to start the new trading week in mostly negative territory.
Stoxx 50 futures seen opening almost 0.1% lower, with all of the continent's major bourses in the red.
The French CAC 40 was almost 0.2% down ahead of Monday's session, while the Italian FTSE MIB was about 0.1% lower.
Futures tied to the U.K. FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX were seen opening around the flatline.
Asian tech heavyweights slid on Monday as investors continued to grapple with the fallout from developments at chip giant Nvidia, with former CEO Jensen Huang reportedly mulling a dramatic comeback.
Key Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company all plunged, with SK Hynix down over 5.6%. Samsung and TSMC lost about 3% each.
AI-related stocks in Japan saw larger losses, with Advantest plunging almost 10% and Tokyo Electron falling 5.2%. Softbank Group Corp , a major AI investor, declined 4.2%.
China's economic slowdown worsened in October with retail sales, investment and industrial output all missing economists' estimates, as analysts warn the growing reliance on external drivers is deepening structural imbalances.
Monday's data showed the investment slump deepened and retail sales again lagged industrial output, as consumer spending languished with the property market downturn eroding household wealth for a fifth year.
The economic malaise also weighed on the labor market. Unemployment inched lower to 5.1% in October, while the jobless rate for those aged between 16 and 24, excluding students, hovered near the highest level in a year, standing at 18% in September.
Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices impacted consumption and net exports.
A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter.
While Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth.
Markets in Asia opened lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 leading losses among the major indexes after its third-quarter GDP unexpectedly contracted.
Nikkei fell 0.63%, while the broad-based Topix dropped 0.24%.
South Korea Kospi fell 0.1%, while the small-cap Kosdaq was 0.56% lower. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.12% as well.
Nikkei 225 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index were set to open higher Monday, with focus on key economic data out of Japan and mainland China.
China is expected to release data for retail sales, industrial output and urban unemployment for October later in the day, while Japan will release economic growth data.
Japan is expected to see GDP growth slow sharply to an annualized 0.3% for the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in the quarter before, according to Reuters estimates.
Japan's Nikkei 225 futures contract in Chicago was at 61,320, compared with the index's previous close of 61,142.35.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,722, compared with the index's last close of 23,637.6.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was marginally lower in early trading.
Energy was the best-performing S&P 500 sector last week, surging more than 5% for its biggest weekly advance since mid-August. Industrials, communications services and tech rose more than 3% each.

Oil prices began the week with a further loss amid reports that the global oil market is returning to oversupply, even as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue and Iraq is forced to export crude by truck via Syria.
Brent crude was trading at $95.24 per barrel at the time of writing, and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $88.31 per barrel, both slightly down from Friday’s close.
The dip followed a report from the International Energy Agency saying that the oil market will swing back into oversupply during the current quarter. The agency cited lower demand, resulting from the higher prices, and the recovery of supply in the Middle East.
Notably, however, the IEA also said that on an annual basis, global oil supply would be 4.8 million barrels daily lower than in 2025, while demand would only decline by 2.7 million barrels daily.
Apparently, traders did not focus on this bit of information, likely because the IEA report was not the only one predicting a return to the glut. Earlier this month, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan analysts both issued predictions of a glut, citing the demand destruction caused by the war between the United States and Israel and Iran.
“We estimate the global oil market returned to a surplus of 1.1 million barrels per day ‌in September, widening to 1.4 million bpd in October, nearly matching last year's average of 1.3 million bpd,” JP Morgan said, while Goldman estimated a balanced oil market for September and October, being more guarded with the glut predictions.
“For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness. That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone,” KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters.
ING commodity analysts, meanwhile, noted that risks remain. “Regional crude flows are approaching pre-war levels, but exports continue to rely on alternative routes around the Strait of Hormuz, leaving supply vulnerable to further disruption,” they wrote in a note at the end of last week.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s wife could land massive divorce settlement, attorney says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s wife could land massive divorce settlement, attorney says
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.”
Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee , whom it did not name. Powell did not respond to the Times, and Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters .
Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort and said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” An FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang is also underway.
Huang has not announced plans to divorce. But a split would test how California divides a fortune built almost entirely on a single stock, and the answer would turn less on his headline net worth than on how the couple’s Nvidia shares were acquired and held.
Huang reported beneficial ownership of about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or 3.58% of the company’s outstanding stock, as of March 23, 2026, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement . Nvidia ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list worth more than $4 trillion .
Jensen and Lori Huang are co-trustees of their living trust, which holds about 528.5 million shares, and of two other family trusts. Together, the three trusts hold nearly 669 million shares. Another 73.3 million shares are held by limited liability companies whose sole member is the living trust.
Lori Huang also runs the family’s philanthropy. She is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, Fortune reported . The foundation holds about 58.7 million Nvidia shares, but the proxy states that neither spouse has a pecuniary interest in them.
The distinction matters. Beneficial ownership and control of shares do not by themselves establish personal ownership, or determine how assets would be divided in a divorce.
The couple met as lab partners at Oregon State University and married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. They live in California, a community-property state, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly and divided equally in a divorce.
“In California, all property acquired by a spouse during marriage is community property,” Christopher Melcher, a Los Angeles attorney who specializes in high-net-worth divorces, told the New York Post . “She would be entitled to 50%.”
Under California Courts guidance , community property generally includes earnings and assets acquired between the date of marriage and the date of separation. Property owned before the marriage or acquired after separation, along with gifts and inheritances, is generally separate property, and some assets can be a mix of both.
That means Lori Huang could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings, not necessarily half of every share tied to her husband.
The outcome would depend on how the shares were acquired, how the trusts are structured, whether separate and community assets were mixed, and whether the couple signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. A court would need to examine those details before deciding what either spouse receives.
California is also a no-fault divorce state , meaning either spouse can seek a divorce without proving infidelity or other wrongdoing. Infidelity, even across several reported relationships, generally does not entitle one spouse to a larger share of community property.
Huang is worth about $145 billion and ranks as the world’s 13th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune reported . That figure is a market estimate, not a tally of marital property, and it rises and falls with Nvidia’s stock, which shed $450 billion in market value in the days after his admission.
Huang has described his wife’s role in the company in plain terms. “Every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview with CNA.

articles.title_orig: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
articles.title_zh: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
articles.content_orig:
On the sidelines of the APEC summit this coming week, Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in hopes of deepening economic and trade ties.
It's the second meeting between the two leaders in less than a year, and this time it will take place in Shenzen, China, where the summit is being held on Wednesday and Thursday.
While Carney has been working to rebuild Canada's economic and trade relationship with China, experts warn that it doesn't mean the threat to Canada has weakened.
Canada's relationship with China might have improved, but the "serious national and economic security threats to Canada ... have not fundamentally changed," said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank with offices in Vancouver and Ottawa.
"What has changed is not China's behaviour but Canada's strategic circumstances and the Carney government's approach," she told CBC News. "With growing uncertainty in our relationship with the United States, there are compelling reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing, pursue economic opportunities and diversify our trade."
Should Canada be engaging with China?
In an interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday, Jody Thomas, national security adviser to Justin Trudeau when he was prime minister, echoed Nadjibulla's views, adding that "the prime minister is pursuing an economic relationship, I hope, and I think with the understanding of the national security threat posed by China."
Speaking to reporters in Montreal on Tuesday, Carney said he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada, adding, "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly."
Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia
Carney said he would be bringing up the importance that Canada attaches "to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries."
The economic and trade relationship between Canada and China "is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we're involved," he said.
It's hard to talk about national security threats from China without pointing to the much-publicized affair between Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia, and an alleged Chinese spy.
For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value . The political ramifications for U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration remain to be seen.
The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips
"What I hope doesn't get lost in all of this is the incredible vulnerability of this kind of concentration in our industry, in our economy and in our politics," former U.S. trade representative Katherine Tai told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.
"How vulnerable you become when you are so reliant on one company that makes one particular product that is apparently there to prop up the major growth industry in your economy. We here in the United States find ourselves in an incredibly precarious place."
Is the Nvidia scandal fracturing Trump's administration?
Carney shared a similar observation at Tuesday's news conference in Montreal.
Referring to China, Carney said, "In terms of the security risks of our partnership, they are much, much, much less than the security risks, for example, [faced by] the United States."
But Nadjibulla said the situation is a bit more nuanced than that.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank, is shown in Ottawa in June 2023. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
While the U.S. and China are "peer competitors" engaged in a global struggle for economic, technological and military leadership, Canada is in a fundamentally different position, she said.
"We are a much smaller, more open economy, with considerably less leverage in dealing with Beijing. That makes us more vulnerable to certain forms of economic coercion and political pressure, not less."
But even then, the question is not whether Canada faces the same level of risk as the U.S., Nadjibulla said. The question is whether Canada has the tools and capacity to manage the risks it does face.
Chinese authorities blocked Canada's Tiananmen Square tribute with trees, cherry picker: documents
Former national security adviser Jody Thomas points to Canada's own recent experience with alleged Chinese spying: the Canadian NATO intern who was arrested in July on charges of espionage allegedly tied to China.
Thomas said that incident and the Nvidia situation shed light on how China operates — but also how Canada needs to adapt to potential threats in the artificial intelligence space.
"What I think it means for Canada is that the approach the prime minister is taking with having a minister responsible for AI, setting up the [ National Council on Artificial Intelligence] , advising in terms of how to use that AI, how to regulate AI and how to ensure that the safety guardrails are developed."
Racy Rafique is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics. She also works as a writer covering federal politics for CBC's parliamentary bureau from time to time. Racy was a 2023 CBC Joan Donaldson Scholar and is a graduate of Toronto Metropolitan University. You can reach her at racy.rafique@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.title_zh: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.content_orig:
It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up.
Ever since 1982, when Ronald Reagan traded a recession, 11% unemployment and Democrats’ 26-seat pickup for a five-day swing through Latin America, Air Force One has been leaving political upheaval behind in its contrail.
President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his authoritarian counterparts from China and Russia — a splashy show of geopolitical theater alongside men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchallenged.
Comparisons with a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable.
The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status. He’ll be joined on the trip by Elon Musk, whose $445 million in political spending failed to deliver Republican majorities.
“Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.”
It’s not the only complication on Trump’s plate. The scandal involving Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips and affair with an alleged Chinese spy will loom over the US president’s visit to Shenzhen, the gleaming hub of China’s tech industry, even though Trump’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey.
Trump doesn’t intend to raise the spying matter with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, American officials have previously told CNN. Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to further restrict high-powered chips from going to China .
“It’s probably not something we’re going to read the Chinese in on at the moment,” one senior US official said.
Never particularly enthusiastic about grueling trips through far-flung time zones, Trump departs for the Philippines Monday after shaking up his West Wing leadership and facing calls even from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense. An air travel meltdown before he left — which Trump did not address publicly for days — also raised new questions about his mindset and focus heading into the trip.
At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in a region that for decades has suffered from Washington’s inattention.
Like his most recent predecessors, Trump has found the “pivot to Asia” an elusive concept. His second term became bogged down by a war in the Middle East, the same region that kept George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden from fully turning American foreign policy toward the Pacific.
Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said.
Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s so-far futile efforts to end the war in Ukraine , continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks this week in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts.
So, too, will Democrats’ stateside victories lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters.
A foreign trip has long been a way to drive home that point while also escaping Washington as the opposition prepares to assume power. Michael Deaver, an image-maker to Reagan, is credited with inventing the tactic when he arranged the Latin America trip in 1982.
Nearly every president since then has replicated the idea. Bill Clinton made a trip to the Philippines in November 1994 after Republicans swept control of Congress for the first time in decades. George W. Bush was in Vietnam a few weeks after the GOP lost Congress in 2006. Barack Obama headed to Asia in 2010 and 2014 after midterm routs. And Trump himself made a somewhat desultory visit to France in 2017 after the GOP lost its majority in the House.
“I’ve been with presidents immediately after midterm, both wins and losses, and it’s always important,” Kagan said. “It’s something that reminds the nation, it reminds foreign observers, that this is very much the president’s bailiwick.”
For Trump, that means appearing in a joint setting with powerful men to discuss the world’s affairs. For some, the meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin carries unpleasant echoes of the 1945 conference in the Crimean resort of Yalta, where Stalin, Churchill and an extremely ill Franklin D. Roosevelt carved up the postwar world into western and eastern spheres of influence.
Putin originally proposed the three-party summit as a venue to discuss the Ukraine war, where fraught issues of borders and sovereignty loom over nascent peace talks.
Trump’s aides insist Thursday’s meeting is nothing of the sort, and say Ukraine won’t even be on the agenda. Instead, Trump hopes to open discussions on nuclear weapons with two leaders he’s worked hard to cultivate. The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia — which each have an estimated 5,000 warheads — expired in February. China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its arsenal to more than 600 warheads but shows little interest in joining a pact.
China’s ‘miracle city’ that no US president has visited (yet)
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said expectations were low for a major breakthrough, describing the talks instead as a starting point.
“It’s time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said.
Xi had initially appeared skeptical of hosting the meeting, officials said, concerned it could overshadow the APEC summit and his attempts to showcase a rising China. But on Monday China’s foreign ministry billed it as meeting of “groundbreaking significance,” with spokesperson Mao Ning saying “such efforts would will help stabilize the global situation.”
Trump, who sometimes says he envies authoritarians who rule as they wish, signed on quickly.

Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair.
Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race.
Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer.
Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below.
Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance.
Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms.
Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips.
In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata . Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company.
Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning.
By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg , and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP .
Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline.
More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times .
State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated  export-control restrictions.

articles.title_orig: Accounting student’s AI cheating sparks South Korean exam furore
articles.title_zh: Accounting student’s AI cheating sparks South Korean exam furore
articles.content_orig:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

Business live – latest updates
Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 165,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.
The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.
US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌chief’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.
Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.
after newsletter promotion
Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.
Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but no date has been set yet.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot says Netanyahu ‘cannot remain’ after alleged election interference by aide
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot says Netanyahu ‘cannot remain’ after alleged election interference by aide
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government , launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government .
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election .
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

articles.title_orig: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
articles.title_zh: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
articles.content_orig:
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.
Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.title_zh: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title_orig: Fire in Phuket shophouse kills 11 injures 16, police say
articles.title_zh: Fire in Phuket shophouse kills 11 injures 16, police say
articles.content_orig:
A fire in ⁠a commercial ⁠building on Thailand’s southern resort island of Phuket has ⁠killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, according to police.
The blaze in the tourist hub of Patong started at about 3:17am on Monday (20:17 GMT on Sunday) in a building housing a restaurant, rented accommodation and a motorcycle rental shop, and later spread to several other buildings nearby.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but an initial investigation found that an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started, ruling out arson.
Phuket Governor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tyres. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
Of the 16 people injured, the authorities said, 15 were Thai and one was a Myanmar national, adding that no tourists were among those injured or killed.
The injured were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and injuries from broken glass.
Thailand’s approach to health and safety regulations, especially in bars and nightclubs has long raised concerns.
In July, a crowded bar in the capital, Bangkok, was engulfed in flames and smoke, killing about 40 people after an electrical short circuit triggered the blaze, authorities said.
Four people were killed and many more injured in a fire that swept through a club popular with tourists on Phuket in 2012.
A fire tore through a Bangkok club during New Year celebrations in 2009, killing 67 people and injuring more than 200.
